newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss to let panel rule on Holocaust assets.
newsitem.headline: Swiss to let panel rule on Holocaust assets.

text.p: Swiss banks, under pressure to speed up the search for accounts left by victims of the Nazis, agreed on Wednesday to let an independent panel rule on claims to Holocaust-era assets.

The banks also said they would publish a first list of pre-1945 dormant accounts on July 23, using the Internet and other media to spread the information internationally so Holocaust survivors or their heirs could come forward.

An independent, international arbitration panel will resolve the claims, according to a joint statement from the Swiss Federal Banking Commission and a joint Swiss-Jewish commission headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker.
It said the panel would be set up quickly with a majority of international members and a Swiss president, but gave no names.
"We want to emphasise that the arbitration procedure is aimed at achieving rapid and definitive results with full justice for the rightful claimants," the statement said.

Bankers, regulators and the Volcker commission have been talking since April about finding a way to speed up settlements because of the advanced age of Holocaust survivors as well as the complexity of tracing claims going back half a century.
It was another move by Swiss banks to hand over decision-making power to outsiders under pressure from critics led by the World Jewish Congress.

Swiss banks last year agreed to WJC demands for the independent Volcker commission, the first such panel in Switzerland empowered to lift bank secrecy rules to allow investigators to go through old files.

Historians from a commission created by the Swiss government in December are also allowed to look through confidential bank records as part of their task of writing a sweeping review of Swiss financial ties with Nazi Germany.

The agreement between the Swiss Bankers Association industry group, Swiss bank regulators and the Volcker commission came as criticism of Swiss banks continued from a Geneva conference hosted by the U.S.-based Simon Wiesenthal Centre.

At the conference on the restitution of Jewish property looted by the Nazis, a prominent U.S. lawyer representing Holocaust survivors said on Wednesday that Swiss banks had acted as "willing bankers for Hitler's executioners and thieves".
Swiss bankers were not present to respond at the conference.
Swiss banks have kept a low profile towards similar accusations from critics, preferring to stress that they are actively seeking to return any accounts left by Holocaust victims.
But the Berne government has vigorously rejected the image of Switzerland as bankers to the Nazis.

In a detailed response last month to U.S. criticism, the Swiss government acknowledged some "questionable deals" during World War Two but defended trade with the surrounding Axis powers as necessary to the small Alpine country's survival.

In a search last year, Swiss banks found about 43 million Swiss francs ($30 million) in dormant accounts possibly held by Holocaust victims. Independent auditors led by the Volcker commission are now conducting another search.
Hausfeld forecast that a U.S. court would hear his case, which seeks in the name of Holocaust survivors to force Swiss banks to throw open their books for possible compensation.

Swiss banks and the government have argued that the proposed class-action suit Hausfeld is leading -- one of three such suits pending -- should not be heard by a U.S. federal court because this would hamper efforts in Switzerland to see justice done.
The next hearing is on July 30 and Hausfeld told Reuters he thought the court would decide to accept the case.

"At this point I am fairly confident that, based on the materials we were able to submit, the court will accept jurisdiction. And then the banks will have to face their responsibility legally as well as morally," he said.
He played down chances of an out-of-court settlement, saying Swiss banks were reluctant to discuss this.

In Berne, the Swiss cabinet on Wednesday approved a plan for the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to contribute 100 million Swiss francs ($69.5 million) to a special humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors.

The cabinet recommended parlaiment approve the move, which would add to 170 million Swiss francs ($120 million) pledged by banks and industry. A public referendum on the matter has not been ruled out.
